motion: This house believes a good question teaches more than a good answer.
motion_sentences: This house believes a good question teaches more than a good answer.

segments.text: Friends, the motion says
a good question teaches more than a good answer

pins.words: This house believes a good question teaches more than a good answer.

segments.text:
. Before I back it, I want to know what "teaches" means here. I suspect the whole sitting hangs on that one word.

Suppose it means putting a true thing into someone's head. Then the answer wins easily. A ship's pilot asks where the rocks are. Tell him. No question, however fine, will save his hull.

Suppose instead it means leaving someone able to find the next true thing alone. Take a teacher with a child at sums. She can say "twelve." Or she can ask, "what happens if you count the rows?" The child who is told has twelve. The child who is asked has twelve, and a way to reach thirteen.

So I have two questions for the house.

1. Which sense of "teach" are we voting on?
2. Can a question teach someone who knows nothing yet? Ask a first-voyage pilot "where might the rocks be?" and you have drowned him.

Where I stand: I support the motion in the second sense, with a limit. A good question teaches more, but only to a learner who already holds enough answers to work with. Questions build on answers; they do not replace them.

What would change my mind is a plain case where being told left the learner better able to go on alone than being asked.

Members of the house, every one of us learned to count and to reason from somebody. Today we decide what we owe them most: their questions or their answers.

I oppose the motion: a good answer teaches more.

I will show two things: that a good answer carries its method with it, and that a question's power is borrowed.

First, a good answer is not a bare "twelve". It is twelve with its reasons. Euclid asks his reader nothing. He lays out proofs, and for some two thousand years students who followed them learned to prove what he never wrote. Broad asked for
a plain case where being told left the learner better able to go on alone than being asked

segments.text:
. I offer geometry.

Second, a question works only on what answers have already supplied. Broad grants this:
Questions build on answers; they do not replace them.

the child who is asked has twelve, and a way to reach thirteen.
